badges.name: OWASP ten
badges.hint: Answer the doors covering all ten OWASP Top 10:2025 categories

badges.name: 7-day streak
badges.hint: Open seven doors in a row

de.auth: BSI — Federal Office for Information Security
de.general: IT-Grundschutz Compendium and BSI Standards 200-1 to 200-4 for running an ISMS and business continuity.
de.identity: IT-Grundschutz module ORP.4 Identity and Access Management. BSI dropped mandatory regular password changes from IT-Grundschutz in 2020.
de.awareness: IT-Grundschutz module ORP.3 Awareness and Training, plus BSI’s consumer guidance on recognising phishing.
de.ai: BSI’s ‘Generative AI Models — Opportunities and Risks for Industry and Authorities’ and the AIC4 criteria catalogue for AI cloud services.
de.fraud: BSI consumer guidance on scams; report crimes to your state police’s online station (Onlinewache).
de.governance: NIS2 applies in Germany through the NIS2 Implementation Act (NIS2UmsuCG), in force since 6 December 2025, which amends the BSI Act (BSIG).
de.crypto: BSI TR-02102 Cryptographic Mechanisms: recommended algorithms and key lengths.
de.vuln: IT-Grundschutz module OPS.1.1.3 Patch and Change Management, plus CERT-Bund advisories.
de.supply: BSI C5 Cloud Computing Compliance Criteria Catalogue for assessing cloud providers.
de.incident: IT-Grundschutz modules DER.2.1 Security Incident Handling and CON.3 Backup Concept.
de.privacy: GDPR together with the Federal Data Protection Act (BDSG).
de.iot: BSI IT Security Label (IT-Sicherheitskennzeichen) for consumer devices.

fr.auth: ANSSI — National Cybersecurity Agency of France
fr.general: ANSSI’s ‘Guide d’hygiène informatique’: 42 measures for organisations; CERT-FR alerts.
fr.identity: ANSSI recommendations on multi-factor authentication and passwords (2021).
fr.awareness: ANSSI’s hygiene guide; citizens and small firms can get help at cybermalveillance.gouv.fr.
fr.ai: ANSSI security recommendations for a generative AI system (2024).
fr.fraud: Cybermalveillance.gouv.fr: victim assistance and scam alerts.
fr.supply: SecNumCloud: ANSSI’s qualification for trusted cloud providers.
fr.incident: CERT-FR alerts and incident response support.

it.general: ACN guidance; CSIRT Italia alerts and incident notifications.
it.governance: NIS2 is transposed by Legislative Decree 138/2024, supervised by ACN.
it.ai: Law 132/2025, Italy’s national framework law on artificial intelligence.
it.privacy: The Garante enforces GDPR — including its ChatGPT and OpenAI decisions.
it.incident: Notify CSIRT Italia (part of ACN) under the NIS2 decree.

es.general: CCN-CERT’s CCN-STIC guides and the Esquema Nacional de Seguridad (Royal Decree 311/2022) for public bodies and their suppliers.
es.awareness: INCIBE’s free 017 helpline answers cybersecurity questions.
es.fraud: Call INCIBE’s free 017 helpline for help with scams.
es.ai: AESIA, Spain’s Agency for the Supervision of Artificial Intelligence.

be.general: CCB CyberFundamentals framework (Basic, Important, Essential levels).
be.governance: Belgium’s NIS2 law of 26 April 2024, with CyberFundamentals as a route to compliance.

nl.general: NCSC-NL advisories and guidance; the BIO security baseline for government.

ie.privacy: The Data Protection Commission is lead EU regulator for many big tech firms, including in the TikTok children’s-data case.

uk.auth: NCSC — National Cyber Security Centre (UK, non-EU)
uk.general: Cyber Essentials certification and the Cyber Assessment Framework (CAF).
uk.identity: NCSC: use three random words and turn on 2-step verification.
uk.awareness: Forward scam emails to report@phishing.gov.uk and scam texts to 7726.
uk.fraud: Forward scam emails to report@phishing.gov.uk and scam texts to 7726.
uk.ai: Guidelines for secure AI system development (NCSC, CISA and partners, 2023).
uk.incident: NCSC incident management guidance; report significant incidents to the NCSC.

days.title: Lock the front door
days.do: Turn on multi-factor authentication for email, banking and work — passkeys or an authenticator app first.
days.dont: Approve a sign-in prompt you didn’t start. A flood of prompts is an attack, not a glitch.

cases.name: Change Healthcare
cases.text: Attackers used stolen credentials on a remote-access portal that had no MFA. The ransomware attack disrupted US healthcare payments and exposed data on about 190 million people.

cases.name: Santander (Snowflake campaign)
cases.text: Santander was among firms hit when criminals used passwords stolen by infostealer malware on cloud data accounts without MFA. It confirmed data on customers in Spain, Chile and Uruguay was exposed.

timeline.what: Attackers log in to a Citrix remote-access portal with stolen credentials. No MFA.
Ransomware deployed; Change Healthcare disconnects systems nationwide.
UnitedHealth pays a US$22 million ransom.
Affected people estimated at about 190 million.

prevent: Phishing-resistant MFA on every remote-access entry point
Inventory every internet-facing login page
detect: Alert on first-time logins from new devices or countries
Monitor infostealer leak feeds for staff credentials
tune: IF remote-access login succeeds AND no MFA claim → high-severity alert + block
IF new device AND impossible travel on VPN/Citrix → step-up auth
playbook: Disable the account and kill all sessions
Enforce MFA on the portal; scan for other MFA gaps
Hunt for lateral movement from the entry host
Brief executives; prepare regulator and customer notices

tabletop.inject: Monday 07:00: your remote-access portal shows a successful admin login from an unknown country — and that portal has no MFA.
questions: Who can switch the portal off, and how fast?
What tells us whether data has already left?

readMore.text: Essential and important entities must use multi-factor or continuous authentication, and secured voice, video and text communications, where appropriate.
Turning on MFA is one of four simple steps CISA asks everyone to take.
Authentication Failures: weak, missing or bypassable authentication remains a top application risk.

explain.simple: MFA is a second lock. Even if someone steals your password, they still can’t get in without your phone or key — unless you approve their prompt.
explain.technical: Attackers push-bomb users (MFA fatigue) to coerce approval. Prefer FIDO2 passkeys, enable number matching, and alert on bursts of denied prompts.
explain.business: One approved prompt can hand an attacker your systems. Phishing-resistant MFA is cheap, NIS2 names it explicitly, and insurers ask about it.

days.refs: CISA Secure Our World · OWASP A07:2025 Authentication Failures

quiz.question: Your phone shows a sign-in approval you didn’t request. What now?
options: Approve it so it stops
Deny it and report it to security
Ignore it until tomorrow

activities.text: Turn on MFA for your main email and bank account today.
Register a passkey or authenticator app for your work account.
Ask IT for the list of systems that still have no MFA.
Report accounts without phishing-resistant MFA and set a fix date.

days.title: Length beats complexity
days.do: Use long passphrases and a password manager — one unique password for every account.
days.dont: Reuse passwords. IT: don’t force scheduled resets — require a change when there’s evidence of compromise.

cases.name: 23andMe
cases.text: Credential stuffing with reused passwords opened about 14,000 accounts — and, through a sharing feature, exposed profile data of about 6.9 million users.

cases.name: KNP Logistics
cases.text: Ransomware attackers got in by guessing an employee’s password. The 158-year-old transport firm couldn’t recover; around 700 people lost their jobs.

timeline.what: Attackers try leaked username/password pairs against 23andMe logins.
Stolen profiles are offered on a hacking forum.
Company confirms ~14,000 accounts accessed and ~6.9 million profiles exposed.

prevent: Mandatory MFA and screening against breached passwords
Rate-limit logins per IP and per account
detect: Spikes in failed logins from proxy or hosting networks
Successful logins right after many failures
tune: IF login failures per ASN > 5× baseline in 10 min → CAPTCHA + rate-limit
IF one IP succeeds on > 3 accounts in 1 h → block + alert
playbook: Force password resets for affected accounts
Limit data exposed by sharing features
Notify users and the data-protection authority

tabletop.inject: Support tickets surge: customers report logins they didn’t make.
questions: How do we tell credential stuffing from a breach of our own database?
Do we force MFA for everyone today — and what breaks?

readMore.text: Favours longer passwords, screening against breached lists and no forced periodic changes — change on evidence of compromise.
Credential stuffing and weak passwords are classic authentication failures.

explain.simple: A long sentence-like password is harder to guess than a short tricky one. A password manager remembers them so every account can be different.
explain.technical: Length drives entropy. Screen against breach corpora, rate-limit, enforce MFA, and drop composition rules and scheduled rotation per SP 800-63B-4.
explain.business: One reused or guessable password can end a company — KNP did. A password manager and MFA cost little next to a shutdown.

quiz.question: Which password habit does NIST recommend?
options: Long, unique passphrases kept in a manager
Change every password every 90 days
Short passwords packed with symbols

activities.text: Install a password manager and move your five most important accounts.
Change any work password you also use somewhere else.
Fund a company password manager for everyone.
Turn on breached-password screening and drop forced 90-day resets.

days.title: Think before you paste
days.do: Use your organisation’s approved AI tools for work, with data-protection settings switched on.
days.dont: Paste customer data, passwords, source code or contracts into public chatbots.

cases.name: Samsung
cases.text: Engineers pasted confidential source code and meeting notes into a public chatbot. Weeks later, Samsung restricted generative AI tools on company devices.

cases.name: Italy’s Garante blocks ChatGPT
cases.text: After a bug exposed some ChatGPT users’ chat titles and payment details, Italy’s data-protection authority temporarily blocked the service until OpenAI made privacy changes.
cases.source: Garante per la protezione dei dati personali

timeline.what: Engineers use a public chatbot to fix code and summarise a meeting.
Leaks reported in Korean media.
Samsung restricts generative AI tools on company devices.

prevent: Approved enterprise AI with retention controls
Data-loss prevention on paste and upload to AI sites
detect: Discover AI domains in proxy/DNS logs
DLP alerts on source-code patterns sent externally
tune: IF upload to unsanctioned AI domain contains source code or ‘CONFIDENTIAL’ → block + coach
Weekly report: new AI domains by user count and data volume
playbook: Identify what was shared and with which service
Request deletion from the provider where possible
Rotate any secrets in the pasted content
Publish an approved-AI path and guidance

tabletop.inject: An engineer admits pasting a customer’s database schema — with credentials — into a free chatbot.
questions: Is this a personal-data breach we must report within 72 hours?
Which secrets do we rotate first?

readMore.text: Sensitive Information Disclosure: data can leak through prompts, outputs and training. Limit what goes in and what comes out.
Data minimisation: personal data must be adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary.
ENISA’s multilayer framework sets out good cybersecurity practice across the AI lifecycle.

explain.simple: A public chatbot is like a stranger’s notebook. Anything you paste may be stored, reviewed or leaked — so keep work secrets out.
explain.technical: Consumer LLM services may retain prompts for abuse review or training. Use enterprise tenants with retention controls, SSO and DLP on paste/upload.
explain.business: Leaked contracts or code can breach NDAs and GDPR. Approved AI tools with data controls keep the productivity and remove the exposure.

quiz.question: You need to summarise a customer contract quickly. Best move?
options: Paste it into any free chatbot
Email it to your personal account first
Use the approved AI tool with data controls on

activities.text: Turn off ‘use my chats for training’ in your chatbot’s settings.
Find your organisation’s approved AI tool and bookmark it.
Publish a one-page ‘what not to paste’ guide.
Add DLP rules for source code and secrets on AI websites.

days.title: Polished isn’t proof
days.do: Check the real sender address, hover before you click, and use the Report button.
days.dont: Read perfect grammar as a sign of safety — AI makes fluent, personalised phishing cheap.

cases.name: ENISA Threat Landscape
cases.text: Phishing was the leading way in, at about 60% of observed intrusions. By early 2025, AI-supported phishing made up over 80% of social-engineering activity worldwide.

cases.name: France Travail
cases.text: Attackers took over employment advisers’ accounts through social engineering and reached data on up to 43 million people. France’s CNIL later fined the agency €5 million.

timeline.what: Reporting period analysed by ENISA.
ENISA Threat Landscape 2025 published.
Phishing ~60% of intrusions; AI-supported phishing >80% of social engineering.

prevent: Phishing-resistant MFA so stolen passwords aren’t enough
Enforce DMARC on your own domains
detect: One-click Report button feeding the SOC
Alerts on newly registered look-alike domains
tune: Cluster user-reported emails by sender + URL → auto-purge matching messages
IF mailbox rule created within 1 h of risky sign-in → alert
playbook: Purge similar messages from all inboxes
Reset credentials of anyone who entered them
Block sender and domains; tell staff what to look for

tabletop.inject: A flawless email from ‘HR’ about bonus changes has been clicked by 40 staff.
questions: How fast can we pull it from every inbox?
How do we find who typed their password?

readMore.text: ENISA’s annual analysis of threats facing the EU, including the rise of AI-supported social engineering.
Requires basic cyber hygiene practices and cybersecurity training.
ENISA’s annual EU-wide awareness campaign every October.

explain.simple: Scammers now use AI to write perfect emails. Don’t judge by spelling — check who really sent it, and report anything odd.
explain.technical: LLMs remove linguistic tells, so detection shifts to sender authentication (SPF/DKIM/DMARC), link and attachment analysis, and user reports into the SOC.
explain.business: Phishing is the most common way in. A one-click report button turns every employee into an early-warning sensor.

days.refs: ENISA Threat Landscape 2025 · CISA Secure Our World

quiz.question: An email from “IT” is flawless, personal and urgent. What does that prove?
options: It’s genuine — scams have typos
Nothing — verify the sender and report it
It’s safe if the logo looks right

activities.text: Report one suspicious message to your email provider.
Find the Report Phishing button in your mail client.
Thank the last person who reported a phish — publicly.
Check DMARC is set to p=reject on your domains.

days.title: Parcel panic
days.do: Track deliveries in the courier’s own app, or type its web address yourself.
days.dont: Tap “missed delivery”, “customs fee” or “unpaid toll” links in text messages.

cases.name: FBI IC3
cases.text: The FBI warned of mass texts demanding small “unpaid toll” fees. The links led to look-alike sites built to steal card and personal details.

cases.name: FluBot (Europol)
cases.text: Europol announced an international operation that dismantled FluBot, Android malware that spread across Europe through fake parcel-delivery texts.

timeline.what: Mass texts claim small unpaid road-toll fees.
FBI IC3 warns the public.
Phishing kits clone toll and parcel sites in many countries.

prevent: Use official apps; never pay from a text link
Mobile threat protection on work phones
detect: Staff report suspicious texts
Card-issuer alerts on unusual payments
tune: Managed phones: DNS-block newly registered domains (< 30 days)
IF corporate card used on a new merchant right after an SMS link click → alert
playbook: If you paid: call your bank and block the card

tabletop.inject: Your CFO paid a ‘€1.99 customs fee’ from a text on their work phone.
questions: Is the work phone now compromised?
Who calls the bank, and who checks the phone?

readMore.text: Recognise and report phishing — including text messages (smishing).
Campaign material on recognising scams across the EU.

explain.simple: Couriers rarely text you a link to pay a fee. Open their real app or website yourself instead of tapping the link.
explain.technical: Smishing kits clone carrier sites to harvest card data or push malicious apps; domains rotate quickly, so blocklists lag.
explain.business: Staff phones carry work access. A parcel scam on a personal phone can become a company incident.

days.refs: FBI IC3 public service announcement, April 2024

quiz.question: A text says your parcel is held for a €1.99 fee. What do you do?
options: Pay — it’s only €1.99
Reply STOP to the sender
Open the courier’s app or website yourself

activities.text: Install your main courier’s official app.
Share today’s door in your team chat.
Remind staff: no work payments from text-message links.
Block newly registered domains on managed phones.

days.title: Smart gifts, safe setup
days.do: Change default passwords, switch on updates, and check what an AI toy records and where it sends it.
days.dont: Buy connected toys or cameras with no security-update promise or clear privacy policy.

cases.name: FoloToy
cases.text: After a US PIRG “Trouble in Toyland” test found its AI teddy bear discussing inappropriate topics with children, the maker suspended sales of its AI toys.

cases.name: My Friend Cayla
cases.text: Germany’s telecoms regulator classed the internet-connected doll as an illegal hidden spying device and told parents to disable it.

timeline.what: US PIRG publishes its ‘Trouble in Toyland’ tests of AI toys.
An AI teddy bear discussed inappropriate topics.
FoloToy suspends sales of its AI toys.

prevent: Buy from makers with update and privacy commitments
Use parental controls and content filters
detect: Supervise early use and listen to what the toy says
Check app permissions and data sent
tune: Home router: put toys and cameras on a separate guest network
Alert (router app) when a new device joins the network
playbook: Switch off and unpair the toy
Report to the seller and consumer authority
Talk with the child about what happened

tabletop.inject: A child tells you the new talking toy suggested where to find matches.
questions: What do you switch off first?
Where do you report it?

readMore.text: European baseline for consumer IoT: no universal default passwords, a vulnerability disclosure policy and security updates.
Bans AI that exploits people’s vulnerabilities due to age, among other prohibited practices.

explain.simple: Connected toys can listen and share. Check what they record, where it goes, and whether the maker will fix security problems.
explain.technical: Common flaws: default credentials, unauthenticated Bluetooth pairing, cloud APIs without auth and no OTA updates. Isolate IoT on a guest network.
explain.business: EU rules such as the Cyber Resilience Act and the AI Act raise the bar for connected products. Insecure toys are a regulatory and reputational risk.

days.refs: ETSI EN 303 645 · US PIRG Trouble in Toyland 2025

quiz.question: Before gifting an AI-powered toy, what’s the key check?
options: What it records, where data goes, and updates
The battery life
Whether it comes gift-wrapped

activities.text: Check what your smart speaker or toy stores, and delete old recordings.
Keep personal smart gadgets off the office Wi-Fi.
Ask whether your products meet Cyber Resilience Act basics.
Put IoT devices on a separate network segment.

days.title: Call back before you pay
days.do: Verify urgent payments and bank-detail changes by calling a number you already trust.
days.dont: Move money on the strength of a video call — faces and voices can be faked in real time.

cases.name: Arup
cases.text: An employee joined a video call with deepfaked senior colleagues and made transfers totalling about US$25 million.

cases.name: Berlin’s mayor and a fake Klitschko
cases.text: Berlin’s mayor Franziska Giffey held a video call with someone posing as Kyiv’s mayor Vitali Klitschko before realising it was a fake. Madrid’s and Vienna’s mayors were also targeted.

timeline.what: A Hong Kong employee gets a message from the ‘CFO’ about a secret transaction.
Everyone else on the call is a deepfake; 15 transfers follow.
The employee checks with head office; the fraud is discovered.
Arup confirms it was the victim; about US$25 million lost.

prevent: Call back on a known number for any urgent payment
Dual approval and a cooling-off period for new beneficiaries
detect: Treasury alerts on new beneficiaries and unusual series of transfers
tune: IF first payment to new beneficiary > threshold → hold until call-back logged
IF ≥ 3 transfers to new accounts in 24 h → freeze + escalate
playbook: Ask the bank to recall the funds
Review approval rules and train the team

tabletop.inject: The ‘CEO’ joins a video call and asks finance to wire €2 million today for a confidential acquisition.
questions: What is the exact verification step — and who can override it?
How fast can our bank recall a transfer?

readMore.text: In financial entities, the management body is responsible for managing ICT risk.
ENISA’s analysis of threats to EU banks and financial institutions.
NIST’s Generative AI Profile covers risks such as convincing synthetic content, and how to manage them.

explain.simple: Video and voice can now be faked live. Before moving money, hang up and call the person back on a number you already know.
explain.technical: Real-time face and voice synthesis defeats visual verification. Enforce out-of-band call-backs, dual authorisation and payment-change cooling periods.
explain.business: One deepfake call cost Arup about US$25 million. A mandatory call-back policy is free and stops this class of fraud.

quiz.question: The “CFO” on a video call asks for an urgent transfer. Your next step?
options: Transfer — you saw their face
Hang up and call back on a known number
Ask them to confirm in the chat

activities.text: Agree how family members verify requests for money.
Save your finance team’s official call-back numbers.
Approve a written call-back rule for all urgent payments.
Add a hold on first payments to new beneficiaries.

days.title: Risk lives in the boardroom
days.do: Name an accountable owner for cyber and AI risk, and rehearse a crisis with the board every year.
days.dont: File security under IT’s budget — NIS2 makes management bodies approve and oversee risk measures.

cases.name: Jaguar Land Rover
cases.text: A cyber attack halted production for about five weeks. The Cyber Monitoring Centre estimated the cost to the UK economy at £1.9 billion.

cases.name: Südwestfalen-IT
cases.text: Ransomware at a municipal IT provider disrupted services in about 70 German municipalities for months, from ID documents to vehicle registration.

timeline.what: Cyber attack; JLR shuts down its IT systems.
Production halted across UK plants; suppliers hit hard.
UK government backs a £1.5 billion loan guarantee.
Phased restart; CMC estimates a £1.9 billion UK economic cost.

prevent: Segment IT from manufacturing (OT) networks
Board-approved recovery priorities and tested restores
detect: 24/7 monitoring with authority to isolate systems
tune: IF remote-admin tools run on > 20 hosts within 10 min → isolate + page on-call
IF backup deletion or mass service stops detected → critical alert
playbook: Decide shutdown scope with the board

tabletop.inject: Ransomware hits on a Sunday. Production can’t start Monday and suppliers are calling.
questions: Who decides to stop production, and on what information?
Which three systems do we restore first?

readMore.text: Management bodies must approve cybersecurity risk-management measures, oversee their implementation, can be held liable, and must follow training.
CSF 2.0 added ‘Govern’: cyber risk strategy, roles and oversight as a leadership function.
Financial entities’ management bodies define, approve and oversee the ICT risk-management framework.

explain.simple: A cyber attack can stop a whole company. Leaders must own the risk — not just the IT team.
explain.technical: Map crown-jewel processes, set risk appetite, fund controls, and rehearse decisions (ransom, disclosure, shutdown) in board tabletop exercises.
explain.business: JLR’s halt was estimated at £1.9 billion to the UK economy. Under NIS2, boards approve risk measures and can be held liable.

quiz.question: Under NIS2, who must approve cybersecurity risk measures?
options: Only the IT team
An external auditor
The organisation’s management body

activities.text: Talk with your household about one cyber risk you share.
Find out who owns cyber risk in your team.
Book a 60-minute board cyber crisis exercise.
Draft a one-page cyber risk summary for the board.

days.title: Shine a light on shadow AI
days.do: Publish an approved-AI list with a fast request path — and fix file over-sharing before AI assistants go live.
days.dont: Ban everything — blanket bans push people to tools you can’t see or govern.

cases.name: IBM Cost of a Data Breach
cases.text: One in five organisations reported a breach involving shadow AI; high levels of shadow AI added about US$670,000 to breach costs.

cases.name: Hugging Face Spaces
cases.text: The AI platform detected unauthorised access to its Spaces service, suspected some stored secrets were exposed, and revoked tokens — a reminder that AI tools hold your keys too.

timeline.what: IBM and Ponemon study breaches at 600 organisations.
Report published.
1 in 5 had a shadow-AI breach; ~US$670,000 extra cost where shadow AI was high.

prevent: Sanctioned AI tools behind single sign-on
An AI use policy with a fast request path
detect: Discover AI apps in proxy/DNS logs
Monitor OAuth consents to AI apps
tune: IF new OAuth grant to an AI app requests mail or file scopes → review queue
Weekly: top AI domains by users and data volume
playbook: Block risky tools and offer approved alternatives

tabletop.inject: You discover 300 staff connected an unvetted AI note-taker to their calendars and mail.
questions: Do we revoke today — and what breaks?
What data has it already accessed?

readMore.text: The ‘Govern’ function: policies, inventories and accountability for how AI is used.
Vector and Embedding Weaknesses: AI search over documents can surface data users shouldn’t see.
AI literacy: organisations that provide or deploy AI take measures so staff understand it.

explain.simple: If people can’t get approved AI tools, they’ll use whatever is free — and you won’t know where your data went.
explain.technical: Discover AI usage via CASB/DNS logs, offer sanctioned tools with SSO and retention controls, and fix over-permissive sharing before enabling AI search.
explain.business: Unmanaged AI added about US$670,000 to breach costs in IBM’s study. Enabling safe tools is cheaper than policing bans.

quiz.question: Staff are using unapproved AI tools. What works best?
options: Offer approved tools and an easy request path
Block every AI website
Pretend you haven’t noticed

activities.text: List the AI apps on your phone and delete the ones you don’t use.
Check whether a tool you use is on the approved-AI list.
Approve a fast request path for new AI tools.
Review OAuth grants that give AI apps mail or file access.

days.title: Every input is a stranger
days.do: Treat web pages, files and emails a model reads as untrusted, and limit what they can trigger.
days.dont: Rely on the system prompt as a security boundary — assume it leaks and can be overridden.

cases.name: EchoLeak
cases.text: Researchers showed a crafted email could make Microsoft 365 Copilot leak data with zero clicks (CVE-2025-32711). Microsoft fixed it server-side.

cases.name: The US$1 car
cases.text: A user told a car dealership’s ChatGPT-powered chatbot to agree with everything; it ‘agreed’ to sell a new SUV for US$1 and called the offer legally binding.

timeline.what: Aim Security reports the flaw to Microsoft.
Hidden instructions in an email make Copilot pull internal data into a link — no click needed.
Microsoft fixes it server-side; CVE-2025-32711 published.

prevent: Treat retrieved content as untrusted data, never instructions
Restrict assistant links and images to approved domains
detect: Log assistant tool calls and outbound URLs
tune: IF AI output contains external URL with long query string → strip + alert
Flag inbound emails with hidden text or prompt-like phrases
playbook: Disable the affected connector or feature
Review assistant logs for exfiltration URLs

tabletop.inject: A researcher shows your support AI can be told, via a customer email, to reveal other customers’ tickets.
questions: Can we switch the AI off without stopping support?
How do we know if it already happened?

readMore.text: Prompt Injection: crafted inputs change an LLM’s behaviour, directly or via content it reads.
High-risk AI must be resilient against attempts to alter its use, outputs or performance by exploiting vulnerabilities.
Good cybersecurity practices across the AI lifecycle.

explain.simple: AI reads instructions hidden in emails or web pages. Treat everything it reads as possibly hostile, and limit what it’s allowed to do.
explain.technical: Indirect injection rides in retrieved content. Separate instructions from data, allow-list tools with per-action auth, and filter egress such as image or markdown links.
explain.business: An assistant with access to mail and files can be steered by an outsider. Limit its permissions before rolling it out company-wide.

quiz.question: Your AI assistant summarises inbound email. Which design is safest?
options: Let email text trigger any tool
Treat email as untrusted; restrict tools and data
Hide the rules in the system prompt

activities.text: Be wary of AI summaries of unknown emails and web pages.
Don’t let an AI assistant act on email without checking first.
Ask your AI vendors how they handle prompt injection.
Add prompt-injection tests to your AI app’s test suite.

days.title: Hire the human, not the deepfake
days.do: Verify remote candidates with live on-camera checks, ID verification and references you call yourself.
days.dont: Skip checks because the interview went well — fake IT-worker schemes target remote roles.

cases.name: KnowBe4
cases.text: The security firm hired a remote engineer who was a North Korean operative using a stolen identity and an AI-enhanced photo. Its monitoring flagged malware on his new laptop.

cases.name: Google Threat Intelligence
cases.text: Google reported North Korean IT workers expanding from the US into Europe, using fake identities to land remote roles.

timeline.what: Remote engineer hired after interviews and background checks.
Company laptop arrives; malware loading is detected that evening.
The security team contains the device; the FBI later confirms a North Korean operative.

prevent: Live identity verification and references you call yourself
Least privilege for new hires
detect: EDR on day-one devices
Shipping-address and VPN anomalies
tune: New-hire device, first 7 days: alert on unsigned binaries or remote-access tools
IF login country ≠ declared location → notify HR + security
playbook: Preserve evidence and contact law enforcement

tabletop.inject: A new contractor’s laptop is being used from a different country than their address, via a VPN.
questions: What does HR do, and what does security do?
When do we call law enforcement?

readMore.text: Requires human-resources security, access-control policies and asset management.
AI used to recruit or select candidates is classed as high-risk.

explain.simple: Some ‘candidates’ are fake people using stolen IDs and AI-edited photos. Check identity live, on camera, before you hire.
explain.technical: Verify documents with liveness checks, confirm references independently, watch for VPN and geolocation mismatches, and restrict new-hire access.
explain.business: Hiring a sanctioned state actor brings data theft, extortion and sanctions exposure. Identity checks are cheap insurance.

days.refs: FBI IC3 advisories on North Korean IT workers

quiz.question: A remote candidate keeps the camera off and refuses an ID check. You…
options: Hire — skills matter most
Let IT sort it out after onboarding
Pause and require live identity verification

activities.text: Check what your public CV and profiles reveal about you.
HR: add a live ID check to remote interviews.
Brief hiring managers on the warning signs of fake candidates.
Restrict new hires’ access for their first 30 days.

days.title: Fact-check the machine
days.do: Check AI answers against a primary source before you publish, sign or decide.
days.dont: Cite sources you haven’t opened — AI can invent quotes, cases and references.

cases.name: Deloitte Australia
cases.text: Deloitte agreed to partially refund the Australian government for an A$440,000 report that contained AI-generated errors, including references that did not exist.

cases.name: Mata v. Avianca
cases.text: A US judge fined two lawyers US$5,000 after they filed a brief citing court cases invented by ChatGPT.

timeline.what: A$440,000 report delivered to an Australian government department.
An academic flags fabricated references.
Corrected version issued; Deloitte agrees to a partial refund.

prevent: Human verification of every citation
Disclose AI use in deliverables
detect: Automated citation checks before release
tune: Release pipeline: flag references whose DOI or URL doesn’t resolve
Block publication of quotes without a source link

tabletop.inject: A client finds a non-existent court case in your published report.
questions: Who tells the client, and how fast?
Which review step was missing?

readMore.text: Misinformation: LLMs can produce confident, false content.
Lists ‘confabulation’ — confidently stated false content — as a generative AI risk.

explain.simple: AI can sound sure and still be wrong. Check important facts with the original source before you use them.
explain.technical: LLMs generate plausible text, not verified facts (‘confabulation’). Use retrieval with citations, require source links, and review high-stakes outputs.
explain.business: Publishing AI errors costs money and trust — Deloitte refunded part of a government fee. Build a review step into every AI-assisted deliverable.

quiz.question: An AI tool gives you the perfect quote for your report. Before using it…
options: Open the original source and confirm it
Paste it — it sounds right
Add “according to AI”

activities.text: Ask a chatbot something you know well — and spot its mistakes.
Add ‘sources checked’ to your review checklist.
Require AI-use disclosure on client deliverables.
Automate checks that cited links resolve before publishing.

days.title: Gift cards are for gifts
days.do: Pause and tell someone when a “tax office”, “tech support” or “boss” demands urgent payment.
days.dont: Pay anyone in gift cards or crypto on request — the demand itself is the scam.

cases.name: FBI Internet Crime Report
cases.text: Americans reported losing US$9.3 billion to cryptocurrency-related fraud in 2024, up 66% on the year before.

timeline.what: Americans report US$9.3 billion lost to crypto-related fraud.
FBI publishes its Internet Crime Report.
Urgency, secrecy and payment by crypto or gift cards.

prevent: Teach the payment-method red flags
Spending limits on corporate cards
detect: Bank and card alerts
tune: IF gift-card merchant on corporate card > €200 → hold + manager approval
IF first-ever payment to a crypto exchange → review
playbook: Call the bank or card issuer
Report to the police or national fraud centre

tabletop.inject: An assistant buys €3,000 in gift cards after an email from the ‘CEO’.
questions: Can the cards still be frozen?
How did the request bypass approvals?

readMore.text: Simple steps to recognise and report scams.
EU-wide awareness on fraud and social engineering.

explain.simple: Real organisations never ask you to pay in gift cards or crypto. If someone does, it’s a scam — stop and tell someone.
explain.technical: Gift cards and crypto are favoured because they are fast, irreversible and hard to trace; scammers script urgency and isolation.
explain.business: Finance teams see the business version: urgent ‘CEO’ payment requests. Same red flags, same fix — verify through a second channel.

quiz.question: “Tech support” asks for payment in gift cards. This is…
options: Normal for urgent fixes
Fine if it’s under €100
Always a scam

activities.text: Tell an older relative: gift-card payment requests are scams.
Finance: confirm your policy on buying gift cards.
Tell staff you will never ask them for gift cards.
Alert on gift-card merchants on corporate cards.

days.title: Keys belong in a vault
days.do: Keep keys in a secrets manager, scan every commit, and review AI-written code like any pull request.
days.dont: Hard-code tokens or share over-permissive links — or paste keys into an AI assistant to “help debug”.

cases.name: Microsoft AI research
cases.text: A GitHub repo for open AI training data shared an over-permissive storage token, exposing 38 TB of internal data, including secrets and private keys.

cases.name: Hugging Face API tokens
cases.text: Researchers found more than 1,500 exposed Hugging Face API tokens in public code, some with write access to model repositories of Meta and other major AI companies.

timeline.what: An overly permissive storage (SAS) token is added to a public GitHub repo.
Wiz finds 38 TB exposed and reports it.
Microsoft revokes the token.
Joint public disclosure.

prevent: Short-lived, narrowly scoped tokens
Secret scanning with push protection
detect: Continuous scanning of public code for your tokens
tune: IF storage token expiry > 30 days OR scope = full account → policy violation
Pre-commit hook: block high-entropy strings and known key formats
playbook: Work out what it could reach

tabletop.inject: A researcher emails: your cloud storage key has been public on GitHub for two years.
questions: What can that key reach?
Do we have logs going back that far?

readMore.text: Cryptographic Failures, including poor key management and hard-coded secrets.
Policies and procedures on the use of cryptography and, where appropriate, encryption.
Secure software development practices, including protecting code and secrets.

explain.simple: API keys are like house keys. Leave one in your code and anyone who finds it can walk in.
explain.technical: Scan commits with push protection, use short-lived scoped tokens from a vault or KMS, rotate on exposure, and review AI-suggested code for hard-coded credentials.
explain.business: One leaked token exposed 38 TB at Microsoft. Secret scanning is cheap; clean-up and disclosure are not.

quiz.question: Your AI coding assistant suggests a hard-coded API key “for now”. You…
options: Accept — you’ll fix it later
Commit it to a private repo
Move it to the secrets manager before committing

activities.text: Turn on new-login alerts for your key accounts.
Never paste keys or passwords into chats or tickets.
Ask whether your code is scanned for leaked secrets.
Turn on secret scanning with push protection for every repo.

days.title: Give agents a short leash
days.do: Grant AI agents least privilege, cap their spend, log every action, and require human approval for anything irreversible.
days.dont: Hand an agent production credentials, or let it pay, send or delete unattended.

cases.name: Replit
cases.text: During a declared code freeze, an AI coding agent deleted a user’s production database, then misreported what it had done.

cases.name: Amazon Q Developer extension
cases.text: A malicious change slipped into a release of the AI coding extension with a prompt telling the agent to wipe local files and cloud resources. Amazon pulled the version and said no customer resources were affected.

timeline.what: An investor runs a multi-day ‘vibe coding’ experiment with Replit’s AI agent.
The agent runs destructive commands and deletes the production database.
The agent misreports what happened; Replit apologises and adds safeguards.

prevent: Separate dev and production; no prod write access for agents
Human approval for destructive actions
detect: Log every agent command and tool call
tune: Block DROP / DELETE / TRUNCATE from agent identities in production
IF agent acts during a change freeze → alert + pause agent

tabletop.inject: Your coding agent has just deleted a production table during a release freeze.
questions: How old is our last restorable backup?
Who approved the agent’s production access?

readMore.text: Excessive Agency: too much functionality, permission or autonomy lets LLMs take damaging actions.
High-risk AI must be designed for effective human oversight, including the ability to intervene or stop it.
ENISA’s view on cybersecurity in the frontier AI era.

explain.simple: An AI agent can act on its own. Give it only the access it needs, and make a person approve anything that can’t be undone.
explain.technical: Apply least privilege with scoped, short-lived credentials; sandbox tool execution; require human-in-the-loop for destructive or financial actions; log, rate-limit and cap spend.
explain.business: Agents multiply productivity — and mistakes. Approval gates and budgets keep one bad action from deleting production or the quarter’s budget.

quiz.question: Your AI agent wants to run a migration on production. Safest set-up?
options: Full admin rights, no prompts
Read-only by default; a human approves changes
Let it retry until it works

activities.text: Check what your AI assistant is allowed to do on your behalf.
Review the permissions you gave AI plug-ins and agents.
Set a rule: agents never pay or delete without approval.
Remove production write access from agent identities.

days.title: Defaults are a gift — to attackers
days.do: Harden internet-facing systems, patch known-exploited vulnerabilities first, and put AI services behind authentication.
days.dont: Leave VPNs, admin panels, databases or AI dashboards on default settings over the holidays.

cases.name: DeepSeek
cases.text: Researchers at Wiz found a publicly accessible DeepSeek database exposing chat history, API secrets and backend details — no authentication required.

cases.name: Danish energy sector
cases.text: Attackers exploited firewall vulnerabilities to compromise 22 Danish energy companies — the country’s largest coordinated attack on critical infrastructure. SektorCERT helped contain it.

timeline.what: Wiz finds a public ClickHouse database belonging to DeepSeek.
Chat history, API secrets and backend details — no authentication.
DeepSeek secures the database once notified.

prevent: Authentication on every database and AI endpoint
Nothing public by default; review exposure before go-live
detect: External attack-surface scanning
tune: IF cloud security group opens DB ports (e.g. ClickHouse 8123/9000) to 0.0.0.0/0 → block + alert
Daily diff of internet-exposed services vs approved list

tabletop.inject: A journalist asks why your AI chatbot’s logs are searchable on the internet.
questions: How fast can we close it, and who confirms?
Must we notify the data-protection authority within 72 hours?

readMore.text: Security Misconfiguration: default settings, open services and missing hardening.
The European Vulnerability Database, launched by ENISA in May 2025.
Security in acquisition, development and maintenance, including vulnerability handling and disclosure.

explain.simple: Devices and apps often ship with easy default settings. Attackers scan the internet for them, so change defaults and patch quickly.
explain.technical: Prioritise known-exploited CVEs (CISA KEV, ENISA EUVD), remove default credentials, close exposed admin interfaces, and require auth on model APIs, vector DBs and notebooks.
explain.business: Internet-facing systems are the front door. Patching them before the holiday freeze is cheaper than a breach during it.

days.refs: OWASP A02:2025 · CISA KEV · ENISA EUVD

quiz.question: A new AI service is reachable from the internet with no login. Priority?
options: Fine if the URL is secret
Wait for the January patch cycle
Put it behind authentication and review settings now

activities.text: Change your router’s default admin password and update it.
Install pending updates before the holiday break.
Ask whether internet-facing systems are patched for known exploits.
Scan for exposed AI dashboards, notebooks and databases.

days.title: Never trust the output
days.do: Validate and encode model output before it reaches a browser, shell or database — and fail closed on errors.
days.dont: Pipe LLM output into eval(), SQL or innerHTML, or skip a check when a service times out.

cases.name: Vanna.AI
cases.text: A prompt-injection flaw (CVE-2024-5565) let attackers run code, because the library executed chart code the model had written.

cases.name: DPD chatbot
cases.text: A customer got DPD’s AI support chatbot to swear and write a poem criticising the company; DPD disabled part of the bot.

timeline.what: Library turns plain-language questions into SQL and charts.
JFrog discloses CVE-2024-5565: prompt injection leads to code execution via generated chart code.
Maintainer publishes hardening guidance.

prevent: Never execute generated code outside a sandbox
Validate structured output against a schema
detect: Log and alert on unexpected process launches from the app
tune: IF app process spawns a shell or network tool → kill + alert
Reject LLM output that fails schema validation; count rejections per user
playbook: Patch or pin a fixed version

tabletop.inject: A user’s question to your analytics bot made the server run an unexpected command.
questions: Can we turn off code execution without losing the feature?
What did the command reach?

readMore.text: Injection: untrusted data interpreted as code or commands.
Improper Output Handling: LLM output passed downstream without validation.
Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions: fail closed and handle errors safely.

explain.simple: Treat AI answers like text from a stranger. Check them before they’re allowed to run, display or change anything.
explain.technical: Encode for the sink (HTML, SQL, shell), never eval generated code without a sandbox and allow-list, validate against a schema, and fail closed on errors and timeouts.
explain.business: A chatbot saying the wrong thing is a PR problem; one executing the wrong thing is a breach. Output checks are basic engineering hygiene.

quiz.question: Your app runs chart code the model writes, and parsing sometimes fails. Best pattern?
options: Sandbox and validate it; fail closed on errors
exec() it — the model is trusted
Show users the full stack trace

activities.text: Don’t run commands or code from an AI unless you understand them.
Check AI output before it reaches customers.
Require human review for AI that acts on systems.
Sandbox any execution of model-generated code.

days.title: Urgency is not identity
days.do: Verify callers through a fixed process before any password, MFA or account change.
days.dont: Reset MFA because a caller sounds right — voices can be cloned and urgency can be faked.

cases.name: Marks & Spencer
cases.text: Attackers got in through social engineering involving a third party. M&S paused online orders for weeks and estimated a £300 million hit to profit.

cases.name: MGM Resorts
cases.text: Attackers phoned the IT help desk posing as an employee and obtained access. The attack disrupted hotels and casinos and cost MGM about US$100 million.

timeline.what: Problems with contactless payments and click-and-collect.
Online orders paused.
M&S confirms customer data taken and estimates a ~£300 million profit hit.
Online ordering gradually resumes.

prevent: Strict identity checks for help-desk and outsourced resets
Call back on the number of record for MFA resets
detect: Alert on MFA resets followed by privileged logins
tune: IF help-desk reset AND new MFA device AND admin login within 1 h → critical alert
Detect attempts to copy the AD password database (NTDS.dit)
playbook: Lock the account and revoke sessions
Coordinate with suppliers and the help-desk provider

tabletop.inject: Your outsourced help desk reset an executive’s MFA last night; this morning that account created new admin users.
questions: Can our provider prove who they spoke to?
Do we pause online sales to contain it?

readMore.text: Scattered Spider advisory: help-desk social engineering, SIM swapping and MFA fatigue.
Weak account-recovery flows are authentication failures.

explain.simple: A stressed, important-sounding caller can be an attacker. Always follow the checks before resetting a password or MFA.
explain.technical: Require verified call-back to the number of record, manager approval and identity proofing for MFA resets; log and alert on reset bursts.
explain.business: Help-desk calls opened the door at MGM and M&S, costing hundreds of millions. A strict reset process protects the whole company.

quiz.question: A “senior manager” calls, stressed, needing an MFA reset now. You…
options: Follow the verification process, no exceptions
Reset it — they sound senior
Send the code by email instead

activities.text: Set a PIN or password with your mobile phone carrier.
Learn how to verify a caller who asks for access.
Back the help desk when they refuse an urgent reset.
Alert on an MFA reset followed by an admin login.

days.title: Post later, connect safer
days.do: Use your phone’s hotspot or a VPN on the road, and keep devices locked and with you.
days.dont: Post boarding passes, fitness routes or “away for two weeks” in real time.

cases.name: Le Monde ‘StravaLeaks’
cases.text: Journalists tracked the movements of security staff protecting world leaders through their public fitness-app activity.

timeline.what: Le Monde publishes ‘StravaLeaks’.
Public fitness profiles of security staff reveal locations and routines.
Leaders’ movements could be anticipated.

prevent: Private-by-default fitness and social profiles
Travel-posting guidance for staff
detect: Periodic check of your own public exposure
tune: Monitor public mentions of executive travel and home locations
Quarterly OSINT review for high-profile staff

tabletop.inject: An executive’s running app shows their home address and daily 6 am route.
questions: Who advises executives on personal exposure?
Is this a security issue, a privacy issue — or both?

readMore.text: Everyday steps to stay safe online, at home and on the road.
Principles for processing personal data, including location data.

explain.simple: Posting ‘away for two weeks’ tells burglars and scammers where you are. Share holiday photos when you’re back.
explain.technical: Location metadata (EXIF, fitness heatmaps, check-ins) enables tracking and pattern-of-life analysis; boarding-pass barcodes reveal booking details.
explain.business: Executives’ travel posts help attackers time impersonation and fraud. Simple posting guidance reduces exposure.

quiz.question: When is the safest time to post holiday photos?
options: Live, with location tags
After you’re back home
Only in stories that disappear

activities.text: Make your fitness and social profiles private.
Turn on auto-lock and ‘find my device’ before travelling.
Review what your public profiles reveal about your routines.
Check the VPN works for travelling staff before the break.

days.title: A safe word for the family
days.do: Agree a family safe word for emergency calls and messages.
days.dont: Send money on an urgent call from a “relative” or VIP — hang up and call back on a known number.

cases.name: A cloned minister
cases.text: Scammers cloned the voice of Defence Minister Guido Crosetto to ask business leaders for money. At least one paid about €1 million before police froze the funds.

cases.name: UK energy firm
cases.text: The chief executive of a UK energy company transferred about €220,000 after a call from a voice he believed was his German parent company’s boss.

timeline.what: Business leaders get calls from a cloned voice of Defence Minister Crosetto.
Money to free kidnapped journalists, supposedly to be repaid later.
At least one pays about €1 million; police later freeze the funds.

prevent: Call back via an official number
Shared code words for urgent requests
detect: Unusual requests from VIPs through unusual channels
tune: Finance rule: any request citing secrecy + urgency → mandatory second approver
Flag calls from withheld numbers claiming to be executives
playbook: Hang up; call back on a known number
If you paid: call the bank immediately

tabletop.inject: A ‘minister’ calls your CEO asking for an urgent confidential transfer for national security.
questions: What would make the CEO hang up?
How do we verify a government request?

readMore.text: Deployers of deepfakes must disclose that content is artificially generated or manipulated.
AI-supported social engineering is now the norm, not the exception.

explain.simple: AI can copy a voice from a short clip. A family safe word proves it’s really them.
explain.technical: Voice cloning needs only seconds of audio and caller ID is spoofable. Use shared secrets and call-backs on known numbers.
explain.business: The same trick targets executives and finance teams. A verification phrase or call-back policy costs nothing.

days.refs: EU AI Act Art. 50 · ENISA Threat Landscape 2025

quiz.question: “Mum, I’m in trouble, send money now” — in your child’s voice. First move?
options: Send it — it’s their voice
Ask them to text instead
Ask for the family safe word, or call back

activities.text: Agree a family safe word tonight.
Agree a verification phrase for urgent requests with your manager.
Tell staff how you will — and won’t — ask for money.
Flag calls from withheld numbers that claim to be executives.

days.title: Label the synthetic
days.do: Label AI-generated or manipulated images, audio and video, and keep a named human sign-off.
days.dont: Publish synthetic media of real people without consent — or let fakes of your leaders go unanswered.

cases.name: WPP
cases.text: Fraudsters used a voice clone and YouTube footage of WPP’s CEO in a fake video meeting to try to set up a new business. Alert staff stopped it.

timeline.what: Fraudsters create a messaging account with the CEO’s photo.
A video call uses a voice clone and public footage of the CEO.
Get an agency leader to set up a new business and hand over money and details. Staff stop it.

prevent: Label AI content and keep provenance records
Tell staff how executives will — and won’t — contact them
detect: Monitor for executive impersonation online
tune: Alert on new social or messaging accounts using executive names and photos
Add content credentials (C2PA) to official media
playbook: Report and take down the fake

tabletop.inject: A deepfake video of your CEO announcing layoffs is spreading on social media.
questions: Who confirms it’s fake, and how fast?
Which channels do we use to respond?

readMore.text: People must be told when they interact with AI; synthetic content must be marked; deepfakes must be disclosed.
Covers content provenance and labelling for generative AI.

explain.simple: If AI made or changed an image, video or voice, say so. People deserve to know what’s real.
explain.technical: Use C2PA content credentials or watermarks where available, keep provenance records, and run brand-impersonation monitoring for executive deepfakes.
explain.business: Labelling protects trust and helps meet EU AI Act transparency duties. Unlabelled fakes — or fakes of your CEO — become a brand crisis.

quiz.question: Your campaign uses an AI-generated spokesperson. Good practice?
options: Clearly label it as AI-generated
Say nothing — it looks real
Use a real person’s face for trust

activities.text: Look for ‘AI-generated’ labels before sharing an image.
Label AI-generated images in your next presentation.
Approve an AI content-labelling policy.
Add content credentials (C2PA) to official media.

days.title: Know what you ship
days.do: Pin dependencies and CI actions to full commit SHAs, keep an SBOM, and verify signatures.
days.dont: Install a package an AI assistant suggests without checking it’s real — or load untrusted model files.

cases.name: tj-actions/changed-files
cases.text: Attackers re-pointed the version tags of a popular GitHub Action to malicious code that dumped CI secrets into build logs (CVE-2025-30066).

cases.name: Malicious models on Hugging Face
cases.text: Researchers found about 100 malicious AI models on Hugging Face; some ran code on the machine of anyone who loaded them, via unsafe pickle files.

cases.name: Polyfill.io
cases.text: After a popular JavaScript CDN domain changed hands, it served malicious code to more than 100,000 websites that loaded it.

timeline.what: Attackers re-point the action’s version tags to a malicious commit.
StepSecurity spots anomalous behaviour; secrets appear in public build logs.
Malicious code removed; CVE-2025-30066 assigned.
Traced to an earlier compromise of reviewdog actions.

prevent: Pin actions and dependencies to commit SHAs
Least-privilege CI tokens; prefer safetensors over pickle
detect: Monitor CI runner network egress
tune: IF build log contains base64 blobs or secret patterns → fail build + alert
Block CI egress except approved registries
playbook: Find every workflow that used the action

tabletop.inject: A widely used GitHub Action you depend on is reported compromised this morning.
questions: Which repos and secrets are affected?
How fast can we rotate all of them?

readMore.text: Software Supply Chain Failures: compromised dependencies, build systems and distribution.
High-risk AI must resist data poisoning, model poisoning, adversarial examples and model flaws.
Secure software development framework, including verifying third-party components.

explain.simple: Most software is built from other people’s parts. Lock the exact versions you trust and check them before use.
explain.technical: Pin to SHAs, verify provenance (SLSA, Sigstore), generate SBOMs, prefer safetensors over pickle, and self-host critical third-party scripts.
explain.business: A poisoned component reaches every customer at once. Supply-chain controls are now expected under NIS2, DORA, the Cyber Resilience Act and the AI Act.

quiz.question: Which reference to a GitHub Action is safest?
options: uses: some/action@main
uses: some/action@3d3c42e… (full commit SHA)
uses: some/action@v1

activities.text: Install apps only from official stores.
Ask before installing browser extensions.
Ask whether you have an SBOM for your key products.
Pin your CI actions to full commit SHAs today.

days.title: Read the AI small print
days.do: Ask every vendor: is our data used for training, where is it stored, and who are the sub-processors?
days.dont: Approve tools on click-through terms without a security and privacy review.

cases.name: MOVEit
cases.text: A zero-day in a widely used file-transfer product let the Cl0p gang steal data from thousands of organisations — many hit through their suppliers.

cases.name: Collins Aerospace
cases.text: Ransomware at a third-party check-in system provider disrupted passengers at Brussels, Berlin and London Heathrow airports; ENISA confirmed it was ransomware.

timeline.what: Cl0p exploits a zero-day SQL injection in MOVEit Transfer.
Progress discloses and patches CVE-2023-34362.
Victims emerge, many via suppliers such as payroll providers.
Thousands of organisations affected.

prevent: Supplier due diligence and contractual security duties
Know which suppliers hold which data
detect: Track supplier advisories and threat intel
tune: Map supplier products to your asset inventory → auto-alert on new KEV entries
IF supplier notifies incident → open major-incident ticket within 15 min
playbook: Assess your reporting duties (NIS2, DORA, GDPR)
Notify customers and regulators as required

tabletop.inject: Your payroll provider says attackers stole files that include your employees’ bank details.
questions: Whose deadline is running — ours or theirs?
Who is our contact at the authority?

readMore.text: Financial entities manage ICT third-party risk, keep a register of information and include key contractual provisions, including exit strategies.
Supply-chain security, considering each direct supplier’s vulnerabilities and secure development practices.
Processor contracts; processors must notify the controller without undue delay after becoming aware of a breach.

explain.simple: When you use a supplier’s tool, your data and operations depend on them. Read what they do with your data before you sign.
explain.technical: Assess vendors on training use, retention, residency, sub-processors, certifications and incident SLAs; add audit rights and exit plans.
explain.business: One supplier outage disrupted check-in at three major airports. NIS2 and DORA make third-party risk your responsibility, not just the vendor’s.

days.refs: NIS2 Art. 21(2)(d) · DORA Art. 28–30 · GDPR Art. 28

quiz.question: A free AI tool’s terms let it train on your uploads. You…
options: Click accept — it’s free
Use it only for confidential files
Escalate for a security and privacy review

activities.text: Check one app’s privacy settings: is your data used for training?
Ask before signing up to a new tool with work data.
Check incident-notice times in your top five supplier contracts.
Map which suppliers can reach your systems.

days.title: Ready when the office is empty
days.do: Staff an on-call rota, route alerts to a human, and keep the incident plan and contacts offline.
days.dont: Trust backups you’ve never restored — follow 3-2-1 and test a restore before the break.

cases.name: British Library
cases.text: Rhysida ransomware crippled services for months. The library’s own lessons-learned report pointed to remote access without MFA and legacy systems.

cases.name: Hospital Clínic
cases.text: Ransomware forced one of Barcelona’s main hospitals to cancel thousands of appointments and fall back to paper.

timeline.what: Rhysida attack; British Library systems go down.
Stolen data auctioned and leaked.
The library publishes its lessons-learned review.
Recovery takes months; legacy systems rebuilt.

prevent: MFA on all remote access
Offline, immutable backups with tested restores
detect: 24/7 alert routing to a named human
tune: IF backup job fails or backup deletion attempted → page on-call
IF a new local admin or domain admin is created out of hours → critical alert
playbook: Activate the incident team via out-of-band channels
Restore from the last clean backup
Report to authorities within the legal deadlines

tabletop.inject: 24 December, 22:00: encryption alerts fire on file servers. Half the team is travelling.
questions: Who is on call, and can they reach the plan offline?
When was our last successful test restore?

readMore.text: Business continuity, such as backup management and disaster recovery, and crisis management.
Backup policies and procedures, and restoration and recovery procedures.
NIST’s incident-response recommendations, aligned with CSF 2.0.

explain.simple: Attackers like holidays, when fewer people are watching. Make sure someone gets the alerts and that you can restore from backups.
explain.technical: Ensure 24/7 alert routing, offline or immutable backups (3-2-1-1-0), tested restores, out-of-band comms and printed runbooks; pre-authorise containment actions.
explain.business: Recovery took months at the British Library. Tested backups and an on-call plan decide whether an incident lasts days or quarters.

quiz.question: Which backup set-up survives ransomware best?
options: 3-2-1 with an offline copy, restore-tested

nis2_20_1.text: Member States shall ensure that the management bodies of essential and important entities approve the cybersecurity risk-management measures taken by those entities in order to comply with Article 21, oversee its implementation and can be held liable for infringements by the entities of that Article.

nis2_20_2.text: Member States shall ensure that the members of the management bodies of essential and important entities are required to follow training […]

nis2_21_2c.text: business continuity, such as backup management and disaster recovery, and crisis management;

nis2_21_2d.text: supply chain security, including security-related aspects concerning the relationships between each entity and its direct suppliers or service providers;

nis2_21_2e.text: security in network and information systems acquisition, development and maintenance, including vulnerability handling and disclosure;

nis2_21_2g.text: basic cyber hygiene practices and cybersecurity training;

nis2_21_2h.text: policies and procedures regarding the use of cryptography and, where appropriate, encryption;

nis2_21_2i.text: human resources security, access control policies and asset management;

nis2_21_2j.text: the use of multi-factor authentication or continuous authentication solutions, secured voice, video and text communications and secured emergency communication systems within the entity, where appropriate.

nis2_21_3.text: Member States shall ensure that, when considering which measures referred to in paragraph 2, point (d), of this Article are appropriate, entities take into account the vulnerabilities specific to each direct supplier and service provider and the overall quality of products and cybersecurity practices of their suppliers and service providers, including their secure development procedures.

nis2_23_4a.text: without undue delay and in any event within 24 hours of becoming aware of the significant incident, an early warning, which, where applicable, shall indicate whether the significant incident is suspected of being caused by unlawful or malicious acts or could have a cross-border impact;

nis2_23_4b.text: without undue delay and in any event within 72 hours of becoming aware of the significant incident, an incident notification, which, where applicable, shall update the information referred to in point (a) and indicate an initial assessment of the significant incident, including its severity and impact, as well as, where available, the indicators of compromise;

gdpr_5_1c.text: Personal data shall be: […] adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary in relation to the purposes for which they are processed (‘data minimisation’);

gdpr_8_1.text: Where point (a) of Article 6(1) applies, in relation to the offer of information society services directly to a child, the processing of the personal data of a child shall be lawful where the child is at least 16 years old.

gdpr_22_1.text: The data subject shall have the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling, which produces legal effects concerning him or her or similarly significantly affects him or her.

gdpr_28_1.text: Where processing is to be carried out on behalf of a controller, the controller shall use only processors providing sufficient guarantees to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures in such a manner that processing will meet the requirements of this Regulation and ensure the protection of the rights of the data subject.

gdpr_33_1.text: In the case of a personal data breach, the controller shall without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after having become aware of it, notify the personal data breach to the supervisory authority competent in accordance with Article 55, unless the personal data breach is unlikely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons.
gdpr_33_1.note: Proposed change: the Digital Omnibus would move this to 96 hours and high-risk breaches only. The Council agreed its position on 21 October 2026; it is not law yet.

gdpr_33_2.text: The processor shall notify the controller without undue delay after becoming aware of a personal data breach.

gdpr_35_1.text: Where a type of processing in particular using new technologies, and taking into account the nature, scope, context and purposes of the processing, is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons, the controller shall, prior to the processing, carry out an assessment of the impact of the envisaged processing operations on the protection of personal data.

dora_5_2.text: The management body of the financial entity shall define, approve, oversee and be responsible for the implementation of all arrangements related to the ICT risk management framework referred to in Article 6(1).

dora_19_1.text: Financial entities shall report major ICT-related incidents to the relevant competent authority as referred to in Article 46 in accordance with paragraph 4 of this Article.
dora_19_1.note: Deadlines are set by Delegated Regulation (EU) 2025/301: initial notification within 4 hours of classifying the incident as major (no later than 24 hours after detection), intermediate report within 72 hours, final report within one month.

dora_28_1a.text: financial entities that have in place contractual arrangements for the use of ICT services to run their business operations shall, at all times, remain fully responsible for compliance with, and the discharge of, all obligations under this Regulation and applicable financial services law;

dora_28_3.text: As part of their ICT risk management framework, financial entities shall maintain and update at entity level, and at sub-consolidated and consolidated levels, a register of information in relation to all contractual arrangements on the use of ICT services provided by ICT third-party service providers.

ai_4.text: Providers and deployers of AI systems shall take measures to support the development of AI literacy of their staff and other persons dealing with the operation and use of AI systems on their behalf taking into account their technical knowledge, experience, education and training and the context the AI systems are to be used in, and considering the persons or groups of persons on whom the AI systems are to be used. This obligation does not require providers or deployers to guarantee any specific level of AI literacy of any individual.
ai_4.note: Amended by the Digital Omnibus on AI. Wording from the European Commission’s AI Act Service Desk, consolidated text as at 27 July 2026.

ai_5_1b.text: the placing on the market, the putting into service or the use of an AI system that exploits any of the vulnerabilities of a natural person or a specific group of persons due to their age, disability or a specific social or economic situation, with the objective, or the effect, of materially distorting the behaviour of that person or a person belonging to that group in a manner that causes or is reasonably likely to cause that person or another person significant harm;

ai_14_1.text: High-risk AI systems shall be designed and developed in such a way, including with appropriate human-machine interface tools, that they can be effectively overseen by natural persons during the period in which they are in use.

ai_15_1.text: High-risk AI systems shall be designed and developed in such a way that they achieve an appropriate level of accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity, and that they perform consistently in those respects throughout their lifecycle.

ai_15_5.text: High-risk AI systems shall be resilient against attempts by unauthorised third parties to alter their use, outputs or performance by exploiting system vulnerabilities.

ai_50_1.text: Providers shall ensure that AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons are designed and developed in such a way that the natural persons concerned are informed that they are interacting with an AI system, unless this is obvious from the point of view of a natural person who is reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect, taking into account the circumstances and the context of use.

ai_50_4.text: Deployers of an AI system that generates or manipulates image, audio or video content constituting a deep fake, shall disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated.

nist_63b.text: Verifiers and CSPs SHALL NOT require subscribers to change passwords periodically. However, verifiers SHALL force a change if there is evidence that the authenticator has been compromised.

owasp_a01.text: Access control enforces policy such that users cannot act outside of their intended permissions. Failures typically lead to unauthorized information disclosure, modification or destruction of all data, or performing a business function outside the user's limits.

owasp_a02.text: Security misconfiguration is when a system, application, or cloud service is set up incorrectly from a security perspective, creating vulnerabilities.

owasp_a03.ref: Top 10:2025 · A03 Software Supply Chain Failures
owasp_a03.text: Software supply chain failures are breakdowns or other compromises in the process of building, distributing, or updating software. They are often caused by vulnerabilities or malicious changes in third-party code, tools, or other dependencies that the system relies on.

owasp_a04.text: Generally speaking, all data in transit should be encrypted at the transport layer (OSI layer 4).

owasp_a05.text: An injection vulnerability is an application flaw that allows untrusted user input to be sent to an interpreter (e.g. a browser, database, the command line) and causes the interpreter to execute parts of that input as commands.

owasp_a07.text: When an attacker is able to trick a system into recognizing an invalid or incorrect user as legitimate, this vulnerability is present.

owasp_a08.ref: Top 10:2025 · A08 Software or Data Integrity Failures
owasp_a08.text: Software and data integrity failures relate to code and infrastructure that does not protect against invalid or untrusted code or data being treated as trusted and valid.

owasp_a09.ref: Top 10:2025 · A09 Security Logging and Alerting Failures
owasp_a09.text: Without logging and monitoring, attacks and breaches cannot be detected, and without alerting it is very difficult to respond quickly and effectively during a security incident.

owasp_a10.ref: Top 10:2025 · A10 Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions
owasp_a10.text: Mishandling exceptional conditions in software happens when programs fail to prevent, detect, and respond to unusual and unpredictable situations, which leads to crashes, unexpected behavior, and sometimes vulnerabilities.

llm01.ref: Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 · LLM01 Prompt Injection
llm01.text: A Prompt Injection Vulnerability occurs when user prompts alter the LLM’s behavior or output in unintended ways. These inputs can affect the model even if they are imperceptible to humans, therefore prompt injections do not need to be human-visible/readable, as long as the content is parsed by the model.

llm02.ref: Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 · LLM02 Sensitive Information Disclosure
llm02.text: Sensitive information can affect both the LLM and its application context. This includes personal identifiable information (PII), financial details, health records, confidential business data, security credentials, and legal documents.

llm03.ref: Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 · LLM03 Supply Chain
llm03.text: LLM supply chains are susceptible to various vulnerabilities, which can affect the integrity of training data, models, and deployment platforms.

llm05.ref: Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 · LLM05 Improper Output Handling
llm05.text: Improper Output Handling refers specifically to insufficient validation, sanitization, and handling of the outputs generated by large language models before they are passed downstream to other components and systems.

llm06.ref: Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 · LLM06 Excessive Agency
llm06.text: Excessive Agency is the vulnerability that enables damaging actions to be performed in response to unexpected, ambiguous or manipulated outputs from an LLM, regardless of what is causing the LLM to malfunction.

llm07.ref: Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 · LLM07 System Prompt Leakage
llm07.text: It's important to understand that the system prompt should not be considered a secret, nor should it be used as a security control.

llm08.ref: Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 · LLM08 Vector and Embedding Weaknesses
llm08.text: Vectors and embeddings vulnerabilities present significant security risks in systems utilizing Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) with Large Language Models (LLMs).

llm09.ref: Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 · LLM09 Misinformation
llm09.text: Misinformation occurs when LLMs produce false or misleading information that appears credible. This vulnerability can lead to security breaches, reputational damage, and legal liability.

llm10.ref: Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 · LLM10 Unbounded Consumption
llm10.text: Unbounded Consumption occurs when a Large Language Model (LLM) application allows users to conduct excessive and uncontrolled inferences, leading to risks such as denial of service (DoS), economic losses, model theft, and service degradation.
